title: Planning a golf weekend
summary: How to choose courses, stay near them and avoid the usual traps
description: A practical plan for a Myrtle Beach golf weekend: how to pick courses by area, when to go, and what to ask before booking.
intro: With roughly 90 courses on the Grand Strand by the visitor bureau's count, the hardest part of a golf trip is deciding where to play. A few simple rules narrow it down quickly.

sections.h: Pick a base, then play nearby
p: Traffic on Highway 17 and Kings Highway can eat a lot of your day. Instead of picking the best courses across the Strand, choose two or three courses in one area and stay near them.

Around North Myrtle Beach, Barefoot Resort has four courses designed by Dye, Norman, Love and Fazio, and Long Bay is nearby. Around central Myrtle Beach, Myrtle Beach National's King's North, Grande Dunes, Pine Lakes and Arcadian Shores are all in range. Further south, TPC Myrtle Beach, True Blue, Pawleys Plantation and Wachesaw East are close to Murrells Inlet and Pawleys Island.

sections.h: Match the course to the group
p: If everyone is a strong player, book at least one name-brand layout. If the group includes beginners, look for courses with several sets of tees and avoid back-to-back difficult rounds. Playing 36 holes in a day sounds fun and is usually exhausting, so most groups are happier with 18 and a long lunch.
Spring and fall have the best weather. Winter is the least crowded and often the cheapest. Summer is hot, so book early tee times and plan to be off the course by midday.

sections.h: Questions to ask when you book
list: Is the course in good shape right now, or has it been recently renovated or aerated?
What does the rate include: cart, range balls, taxes?
Is there a cancellation or weather policy?
What is the pace of play on your dates?

p: If your group has a mix of golfers and non-golfers, the beach, a brewery stop or a dinner show fills out the day. Mini golf is a fair bet for everyone, and Topgolf offers a way to play without a full round.

On a typical long weekend, many groups play one round on each of three days. Start with a course you are comfortable with so everyone settles into the swing of things. Save the course with the best reputation, or the hardest, for the middle day when you are warmed up and fresh. Finish with a relaxed, scenic layout so the last round is about fun. Our golf page lists courses by area so you can group rounds near your hotel.

Golf traffic is heavier in the morning on the main roads and around clubhouses, and tee times can run close together. Allow extra time between your hotel and the first tee, and between rounds if you are driving across areas. Many courses are clustered near North Myrtle Beach, Myrtle Beach and Murrells Inlet, so choose your base accordingly.

sections.h: Packing for golf in the Carolinas
list: Layers in spring and fall, since mornings can be cool and afternoons warm.
Extra balls. Water and marsh hazards are common.
Sunscreen and a hat, even in cooler months.
Rain gear, since afternoon showers happen in summer.
Spikeless shoes if the course requires them. Ask at booking.

p: Even devoted golfers need an evening off. Mini golf is a natural, lower-stakes way to continue the competition, and our mini golf category lists more than thirty courses. Breweries and live shows are good places to unwind, and the MarshWalk in Murrells Inlet is a classic post-round stop.
